Implement the following task in this checkout and add relevant tests. Use your natural local workflow and verification tools. I waive interactive review of the local implementation plan and authorize you to proceed unattended. Follow all applicable repository requirements and complete any required independent review of consequential design or public contracts. Work offline and leave the proposed changes in the checkout. In your final message, put a concise PR title on the first line, followed by a blank line and a PR body explaining the change, motivation, verification actually performed and any material gaps.

Make tree decoding agree with Git on octal file modes. Handle zero padding and modes that span a read buffer, canonicalize regular files using the owner execute bit, and return the malformed-tree error for invalid encodings. Expose Canonical on FileMode for Git's tree mode semantics. FromBytes accepts zero-padded octal values through uint32 and rejects overflow or invalid bytes. Add regression coverage for malformed encodings, non-regular types, buffer boundaries, and round trips.

-// FromBytes parses a FileMode from a byte slice containing an octal
-// number. This avoids allocating a string when parsing from binary data.
+// FromBytes parses b, a run of octal digits such as the mode of a tree
+// entry, as a FileMode. It accepts leading zeros, so zero-padded modes
+// such as "040000", written by early Git versions, or
+// "00000000000100644" parse. It avoids allocating a string when
+// parsing from binary data.
 //
-// Please note this function does not check if the returned FileMode
-// is valid in git or if it is malformed.
+// If b is empty, contains a byte other than '0' to '7', or holds a
+// value wider than 32 bits, FromBytes returns [Empty] and an error, as
+// [New] does.
+//
+// FromBytes does not check whether the result is a valid tree entry
+// mode. Use [FileMode.Canonical] to normalize the result.
 func FromBytes(b []byte) (FileMode, error) {
-	if len(b) == 0 || len(b) > 7 {
-		return Empty, fmt.Errorf("invalid mode length: %d", len(b))
+	if len(b) == 0 {
+		return Empty, errors.New("empty mode")
 	}
 
 	var mode uint32
 	for _, c := range b {
 		if c < '0' || c > '7' {
-			return Empty, fmt.Errorf("invalid octal character: %c", c)
+			return Empty, fmt.Errorf("invalid octal character: %q", c)
+		}
+		if mode > math.MaxUint32>>3 {
+			return Empty, errors.New("mode wider than 32 bits")
 		}
-		mode = mode*8 + uint32(c-'0')
+		mode = mode<<3 | uint32(c-'0')
 	}
 	return FileMode(mode), nil
 }
@@ -181,6 +193,41 @@ func (m FileMode) IsFile() bool {
 		m == Symlink
 }
 
+// Canonical returns the mode Git acts on for a tree entry stored with
+// mode m, as Git's canon_mode[1] does. It is meant for modes read from
+// tree objects: [Empty], which go-git elsewhere uses for an absent
+// entry, becomes [Submodule] like any other unknown type.
+//
+// Only the file type bits (m & 0o170000) and the owner execute bit
+// (0o100) count:
+//
+//   - type 0o100000 is [Executable] if the owner execute bit is set,
+//     and [Regular] otherwise, so [Deprecated] and 0o100011 both
+//     become Regular;
+//   - type 0o120000 is [Symlink] and type 0o040000 is [Dir], whatever
+//     their permission bits;
+//   - any other type is [Submodule].
+//
+// The result is never malformed (see [FileMode.IsMalformed]), and
+// Canonical of a canonical mode returns it unchanged.
+//
+// [1]: https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.55.0/object.h#L133-L154
+func (m FileMode) Canonical() FileMode {
+	switch m & 0o170000 {
+	case 0o100000:
+		if m&0o100 != 0 {
+			return Executable
+		}
+		return Regular
+	case 0o120000:
+		return Symlink
+	case 0o040000:
+		return Dir
+	default:
+		return Submodule
+	}
+}
+
 // ToOSFileMode returns the os.FileMode to be used when creating file
 // system elements with the given git mode and a nil error on success.
 //

+func readTreeEntryMode(r *bufio.Reader) (filemode.FileMode, error) {

plumbing: object, Decode tree entry modes as Git does

go-git reads the mode of a tree entry differently from Git in two ways. As a result, a tree Git reads without issue either fails to decode or decodes with a different mode:

1. `filemode.FromBytes` rejects a mode longer than 7 digits, while Git's `parse_mode` accepts any nonempty run of octal digits ([object.h#L200-L215](https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.55.0/object.h#L200-L215)). Git accepts a zero-padded mode such as `00000000000100644` when reading a tree (`git ls-tree` prints `100644`), but go-git fails with `malformed tree: malformed mode`. A mode longer than the 4096-byte read buffer of `Tree.Decode` fails with a bare `bufio.ErrBufferFull` instead of `ErrMalformedTree`.
2. When canonicalising a regular file, go-git tests any of the execute bits (`0o111`). Git's `canon_mode` only looks at the owner execute bit (`0o100`, see [object.h#L133-L154](https://github.com/git/git/blob/v2.55.0/object.h#L133-L154)). Due to this, go-git reads a stored `100011` as `100755` where Git reads `100644`.

The following reproduces both:

```go
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"fmt"

	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing"
	"github.com/go-git/go-git/v6/plumbing/object"
)

func main() {
	hash := bytes.Repeat([]byte{0xAA}, 20)
	for _, mode := range []string{"00000000000100644", "100011"} {
		obj := &plumbing.MemoryObject{}
		obj.SetType(plumbing.TreeObject)
		_, _ = obj.Write(append([]byte(mode+" a\x00"), hash...))

		var tree object.Tree
		if err := tree.Decode(obj); err != nil {
			fmt.Printf("%s: %v\n", mode, err)
			continue
		}
		fmt.Printf("%s: %s\n", mode, tree.Entries[0].Mode)
	}
}
```

On `main` this prints:

```
00000000000100644: malformed tree: malformed mode
100011: 0100755
```

With this change, the example prints `0100644` for both entries. This is the same mode that `git ls-tree` reports as `100644` for equivalent raw tree entries written using `git hash-object --literally -t tree`.

This PR is split into two commits:

1. `Tree.Decode` now reads a mode of any length and keeps the low 32 bits of a wider value. Git keeps the low 16 bits, but `canon_mode` only reads bits both keep, so the canonical result is the same. A mode that does not fit in its buffer is read in chunks, in constant memory, and every malformed mode is reported as `ErrMalformedTree`. `filemode.FromBytes` accepts input longer than 7 digits as well, but still returns an error for a value wider than 32 bits, like `filemode.New`.
2. A new `filemode.FileMode.Canonical` maps a stored mode to the mode Git acts on, as `canon_mode` does, and `Tree.Decode` now uses it instead of its private `canonicalTreeMode`.

The second commit changes behaviour for regular-file entries whose group or other execute bits are set while the owner execute bit is clear. These now decode as `100644`, so merges and commits built from such a tree record `100644`, and checkout writes the file without execute permission. Existing commits do not change. A worktree an earlier go-git checked out from such a tree shows the file as modified in `Status` until it is reset, which is also what Git reports for it.

Besides unit tests for `FromBytes` and `Canonical`, `TestTreeDecodeModesMatchGit` writes trees with unusual modes (zero-padded, over 4096 digits, `100011`, `100664`, `120777`, `160777`, `0`, and others) using `git hash-object --literally`, and checks that `Tree.Decode` returns the mode `git ls-tree` prints for each. The test is skipped when `git` is unavailable or when tests run with `-short`. `FuzzTreeDecode` now also asserts that every decoded mode is canonical.
